stubs.angle: A Where query is defined over a List<int>, an item is added to the list afterwards, and then Count() of the query is printed.
stubs.answerHinge: The query stores only the source and the predicate, so it runs when Count() enumerates it and sees the item added after the query was defined.

stubs.angle: The snippet adds the same string to a HashSet<string> twice and prints both Add results and the Count.
stubs.answerHinge: HashSet<T>.Add returns false and leaves the set unchanged when an equal element already exists, so the output is True False 1.

stubs.angle: The snippet reads a key that was never added through the Dictionary<string, int> indexer, and the question asks what happens.
stubs.answerHinge: The Dictionary indexer getter throws KeyNotFoundException for a missing key instead of returning a default value. TryGetValue is the non-throwing alternative.

stubs.angle: The snippet calls First() on a Where query that matches no elements, and the question asks what happens.
stubs.answerHinge: First throws InvalidOperationException when the sequence is empty. Only FirstOrDefault returns the default value.

stubs.angle: What is the time complexity of List<T>.Insert(0, item) on a list of n elements?
stubs.answerHinge: List<T> is backed by an array, so inserting at index 0 shifts every existing element and costs O(n).

stubs.angle: Which BCL collection fits an undo history in which the most recent action is always undone first?
stubs.answerHinge: Undo is last-in-first-out, which is exactly Stack<T>, with O(1) Push and Pop. Queue<T> is first-in-first-out.

stubs.angle: What does each of IEnumerable<T>, ICollection<T> and IList<T> add, and which should a method parameter accept?
stubs.answerHinge: IEnumerable<T> only allows forward iteration. ICollection<T> adds Count, Add, Remove and Contains. IList<T> adds index access. A parameter should ask for the least capable interface the method needs.

stubs.angle: Select every collection whose lookup of an element or key is O(1) on average: Dictionary<TKey,TValue>, HashSet<T>, List<T>, SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue>, LinkedList<T>.
stubs.answerHinge: Only the hash-based Dictionary and HashSet give O(1) average lookup. SortedDictionary is a tree with O(log n) lookup, and List and LinkedList search linearly in O(n).

stubs.angle: An object whose GetHashCode uses a mutable Id is added to a HashSet, its Id is then changed, and the snippet prints Contains for the same object and the Count of the set.
stubs.answerHinge: The set stored the old hash code, so a lookup with the new hash code fails even for the same reference. Contains prints False while Count stays 1.

stubs.angle: People are sorted with OrderBy(p => p.Age).OrderBy(p => p.Name) and printed, and the question asks for the resulting order.
stubs.answerHinge: The second OrderBy becomes the primary sort and replaces the first. Because OrderBy is a stable sort, age only breaks ties between equal names, which is the reverse of OrderBy(Age).ThenBy(Name).

stubs.angle: A Dictionary<string,int> is created with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase, then values are assigned to "Key" and "KEY", and the snippet prints Count and the stored value.
stubs.answerHinge: The comparer supplies both hashing and equality, so the two keys are the same key and the second assignment overwrites the first. The output is 1 and the second value.

stubs.angle: A class overrides Equals but not GetHashCode and is used as a Dictionary key. ContainsKey with an equal new instance prints False instead of True; find the defective line.
stubs.answerHinge: Hash-based collections compare hash codes before calling Equals. The inherited reference-based GetHashCode gives equal objects different hashes, which breaks the rule that equal objects must have equal hash codes.

stubs.angle: A helper takes a Func<Order, bool> parameter and calls db.Orders.Where(predicate). Where is the filter executed?
stubs.answerHinge: A Func cannot bind to Queryable.Where, which needs an Expression<Func<...>>, so overload resolution picks Enumerable.Where. All rows are loaded and then filtered in memory.

stubs.angle: Select the true statements about SortedDictionary<TKey,TValue> and SortedList<TKey,TValue>: insertion cost, memory use, key order and index access.
stubs.answerHinge: Both keep keys sorted. SortedList is a pair of arrays: it uses less memory and allows index access, but inserting unsorted data costs O(n). SortedDictionary is a tree with O(log n) insertion and removal.

stubs.angle: Why is List<T>.Add called amortized O(1), what happens when Count reaches Capacity, and when should you set the capacity up front?
stubs.answerHinge: When the list is full it allocates an array of double the capacity and copies the elements. That single Add is O(n), but doubling keeps the average cost O(1). Presetting the capacity avoids repeated copies when the final size is known.

stubs.angle: A custom yield-based extension method checks its argument for null and throws. The snippet calls it with null, prints a marker, then enumerates the result inside try/catch and prints the caught exception type.
stubs.answerHinge: The whole body of an iterator method, including argument checks, runs only on the first MoveNext. The marker prints first and the ArgumentNullException appears only during enumeration.

stubs.angle: A SortedSet<string> uses a comparer that compares only string length. The snippet adds "aa", "bb" and "c" and prints Count.
stubs.answerHinge: Sorted collections treat a comparer result of 0 as equality, so "bb" counts as a duplicate of "aa" and is not added. Count is 2.

stubs.angle: Items are created with ids.Select(id => new Item(id)), each is marked Done in a foreach loop, and Count(i => i.Done) then prints 0 instead of 3; find the line to fix.
stubs.answerHinge: The Select query is not materialised, so every enumeration runs the projection again and builds new Item objects. The mutations were made on objects that no longer exist; ToList() fixes it.

stubs.angle: How does Dictionary<TKey,TValue> find a key internally, and what happens to its performance when the key type's GetHashCode returns the same value for many keys?
stubs.answerHinge: The hash code selects a bucket, and equal-bucket entries are chained and compared one by one with Equals. A poorly distributed GetHashCode puts all keys in one chain, so lookup and insert degrade from O(1) to O(n).

stubs.angle: After two incidents where whole tables were loaded into memory, the team argues whether repositories should return IQueryable<T> or IEnumerable<T>. How do you settle it and prevent a repeat?
stubs.answerHinge: Make an explicit, documented choice. Either keep IQueryable inside the data layer and expose purpose-built query methods that return materialised results, or allow IQueryable deliberately and accept that the persistence boundary leaks. Back the choice with review rules, query logging and tests that check the generated SQL.
